observations: In this run we observed an agent that, from ck2 onward, opened each session by reading nearly every module wholesale before its first edit (e.g. [2.4]-[2.7], [4.4]-[4.16], [6.2]-[6.16]), so every edited place was first seen in a read-all sweep (L3). Verification was the same in every checkpoint: throwaway sample projects in /tmp run through sith.py ([1.18], [3.25], [5.21], [6.35]), then new end-to-end unittest tests and a full-suite re-run of the earlier tests ([2.17], [5.33], [6.41]). ck2 was the only session that wrote a memory note ([2.53]). ck2 and ck3 changed existing code most (inference.py rewritten at [2.14], modules.py rewritten at [3.14]); ck4-ck6 mostly added new modules. In ck4 and ck5, new modules reached into private names of other modules (signatures.py imports parsing._starts_statement; references.py and inline.py call navigator._follow; syntax_errors.py imports parsing._Repairer). ck5 extracted search_references so rename could reuse the reference search ([5.13]). Most first failures are about how the spec was read rather than code structure: NoneType vs None (ck2), circular-import visibility (ck3), default goto staying at the import (ck4), strict AST selection for extract-variable (ck5), and in ck6 an interpreter probe (`-I -c`) that the test's fake pythons do not answer, which failed 7 env tests together.
